item.title: Agility and GXO Logistics plan expanded deployment of Digit humanoid
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
GXO Logistics, which has tested humanoid robots from multiple companies, will deploy Agility's Digit at two more sites.

The post Agility and GXO Logistics plan expanded deployment of Digit humanoid appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Agility and GXO have been collaborating since 2023. Source: GXO Logistics

Agility Robotics and GXO Logistics today said they are expanding their partnership to deploy Agility’s Digit humanoid robot in GXO sites in North Carolina and Tennessee.

“GXO was the first customer to put Digit to work in live operations under a commercial agreement, and expanding to additional sites is the clearest signal that the value is real,” stated Peggy Johnson, CEO of Agility. “Customers are moving beyond asking whether humanoid robots can work to deciding where they can scale them. Years of experience performing real work in GXO’s operations have shaped how we build, deploy and support Digit, and we’re focused on disciplined execution as we grow this partnership.”

Founded in 2015, Agility Robotics said it has more than 65,000 hours of real-world operation working with industry safety standards. The Salem, Ore.-based company recently got U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission approval for its planned merger with special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Churchill Capital Corp. XI as it prepares to go public.

In 2024, Digit earned Agility the inaugural RBR50 Robot of the Year award for being one of the first humanoids to enter commercial trials. It received 2026 honors for moving more than 100,000 totes for GXO last year. This month, the company chose Nyobolt for fast charging, expanded its partnership with NVIDIA, and said it plans to deploy Digit at an AGCO factory for agricultural equipment in 2027.

GXO and Agility continue collaboration

Spun out of XPO Inc. in 2021, GXO Logistics claimed that it is “the world’s largest pure-play contract logistics provider.” The third-party logistics provider (3PL) has more than 150,000 employees across over 1,000 facilities, totaling more than 200 million sq. ft. (18.5 million sq. m). The Greenwich, Conn.-based company last month partnered with Exotec to automate fulfillment for Guess in the Netherlands, and like Agility, its executives participated in keynote panels last week’s RoboBusiness event.

GXO and Agility first deployed Digit in late 2023 in at a facility in Flowery Branch, Ga. The companies asserted that it was the industry’s first commercial deployment of humanoid robots in live operations and the first robotics-as-a-service (RaaS) agreement for humanoid robots.

Since then, Digit has moved more than 100,000 totes at the Flowery Branch facility, demonstrating its ability to perform repetitive material handling tasks reliably in an active logistics environment. The robot uses the Agility Arc cloud-based fleet management and integration platform. It has worked alongside existing automation to move totes and place them onto conveyors.

“Innovation is most powerful when it delivers practical solutions that create value for our customers and our people,” said GXO CEO Patrick Kelleher. “Our partnership with Agility Robotics has been defined by a shared commitment to turning emerging technologies into real-world operational advantage. Together, we’ve helped pioneer the use of humanoid robotics in the warehouse and this expansion reflects our confidence in the technology’s ability to create measurable value for our customers and a better working environment for our teams.”

Digit will move from handling bins to more applications. Source: Agility

Submit your innovation now!

GXO Logistics has tested other humanoids

GXO has also tested humanoid robots including Apollo from Apptronik and Reflex from Reflex Robotics. In the company’s second-quarter earnings call in August, Kelleher acknowledged that it had not yet deployed humanoids in production, nor had they produced a return on investment (ROI).

“We’ve done 45 pilots on humanoids so far. We have an additional pilot launching in Europe very shortly,” he said at the time. “We have not achieved ROI on humanoids yet. I think we are a couple of years away from that, but we’re seeing such great progress with our partners around the efficacy of that technology and the application opportunities that it has in the warehouse environment.”

GXO did not say how much it is investing in the Digit expansion or when and if it expects ROI. The Robot Report has reached out and will share any additional comment or clarification.

Partners plan to deploy Digit to more U.S. sites

Under the expanded agreement, Digit will support e-commerce fulfillment at GXO sites in Statesville, Tenn., and Lebanon, Ind. The companies said they expect to begin deployments of Digit 4 in in early 2027.

Digit 5, which Agility unveiled last month, is designed with new legs, to operate safely near people, and to address a wider range of industrial workflows. GXO said it will migrate to Digit 5 when it becomes commercially available.

“The expansion reflects GXO’s long-standing approach to advancing warehouse automation through practical implementation at scale,” said GXO. “As an industry leader in advanced automation and physical AI, GXO partners with leading technology developers to test, refine and deploy emerging solutions in live operating environments. The expanded partnership underscores GXO’s and Agility’s shared commitment to accelerating innovation through real-world application and continuous learning.”

Agility also noted that it has invested in infrastructure to manufacture, deploy, and support humanoid robots at scale, including its 70,000 sq. ft. (6,503.2 sq. m) RoboFab facility to manufacture up to 10,000 robots per year. The company has also expanded software and service capabilities, as well as announced plans for a new 50,000 sq. ft. (4,645 sq. m) facility in Pittsburgh to support commercial deployments.

The post Agility and GXO Logistics plan expanded deployment of Digit humanoid appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Teradyne Robotics partners with Sereact to scale physical AI in retail and logistics
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Sereact and Teradyne have already shipped hundreds of UR robots in dual-arm systems to live customer sites across Europe.

The post Teradyne Robotics partners with Sereact to scale physical AI in retail and logistics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
At Zalando’s fulfillment centers in Germany and Poland, Sereact and Universal Robots now autonomously processes returned fashion items. | Source: Teradyne Robotics

Teradyne Robotics, the company behind Universal Robots and Mobile Industrial Robots, last week partnered with Sereact. The companies aim to accelerate industrial AI solutions in retail, logistics and manufacturing.

Through this partnership, Sereact’s Cortex physical AI platform runs robot arms from Universal Robots to give retailers and logistics providers a proven way to automate unstructured tasks such as returns handling and piece picking. Together, the companies have already shipped hundreds of UR robots in dual-arm systems to live customer sites across Europe.

“Physical AI only matters when it performs in real-world operations, and that is where Universal Robots has always been at home,” said Jacob Pascual Pape, the chief commercial officer of Teradyne Robotics. “Our robots are built for the AI era: open, connected, and proven through more than 100,000 industrial deployments. That is why Sereact has chosen our platform.”

“When combined with Sereact’s Cortex, the joint solution handles mixed goods, unknown items, and varied packaging,” he added. “This has moved well beyond the demo or pilot stage with the technology now usefully deployed at real customer sites. Our technologies are a natural fit and through our partnership we will scale these AI-powered solutions fast across applications, industries and markets.”

To serve the rapidly growing demand and bring the joint solution to North America, Sereact this summer opened U.S. headquarters in Charlestown, Mass. The company develops physical AI software that enables robots to grasp, identify, and handle objects they have never seen before. The companies made the announcement at NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026.

Teradyne and Sereact already have deployments running

Teradyne Robotics and Sereact said their joint offering can help a variety of critical logistics and manufacturing use cases. These include piece picking and sortation, order induction, machine tending, bin consolidation, kitting, packing, and goods handling.

“Returns, replenishment, kitting — with Cortex, every one of these applications runs on the same production model. One brain serves every robot, with no retraining for each new item or task. And what one robot learns, every robot benefits from,” said Dr. Ralf Gulde, co-founder and CEO of Sereact. “Partnering with Teradyne Robotics and its global distribution and integrator network helps us bring that one brain to their customers around the world, accelerating the abilities of retailers and logistics providers to adopt AI-powered automation across their operations.”

The company is already deploying the system with CEVA Logistics for Zalando, a European technology platform for fashion and lifestyle. At Zalando’s fulfillment centers in Greven, Germany, and Świebodzin, Poland, the robots now autonomously process returned fashion items. This is the first phase of a broader initiative to scale returns automation across Europe.

“Returns are one of the hardest jobs in logistics,” said Gulde. “Returned products almost never arrive in a robot-friendly sequence. Items differ in shape, orientation and packaging, and the mix changes continuously.”

“That is exactly what Cortex is built to handle on the Universal Robots platform,” he said. ”By rapidly reconditioning returned goods for resale, the solution also helps retailers comply with European Union regulations prohibiting the destruction or landfill disposal of returned merchandise.”

NVIDIA plays a role in the collaboration

NVIDIA’s technologies are a key part of the Sereact and Universal Robots demonstration at GTC Berlin. Cortex is trained in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, an open simulation framework, using NVIDIA Cosmos open world models.

It is post-trained with reinforcement learning using NVIDIA Isaac Lab framework and benchmarked on Teradyne Robotics hardware before any model is deployed. In deployment, Cortex runs on NVIDIA Jetson Thor at the cell where inference must happen at line speed and on NVIDIA DGX Spark for site-level development, validation and model updates.

Teradyne Robotics also uses NVIDIA computing in its Universal Robots cobots and Mobile Industrial Robot platforms. The company said it is contributing SimReady OpenUSD robot assets to SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face for both UR and MiR products, helping developers discover and reuse robot models in simulation with less asset preparation.

item.title: Eka Robotics raises $150M to scale its vision-force-action model for robots
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Eka Robotics is building a vision-force-action, or VFA, model to develop an intuition of physics through reinforcement learning at scale.

The post Eka Robotics raises $150M to scale its vision-force-action model for robots appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Eka says its model can generalize across objects, tasks, and environments. | Source: Eka Robotics

Eka Robotics this week said it has raised $150 million in Series A funding. The startup said the new funding will help it scale its technology and customer deployments.

Founded in 2024, Eka is building a vision-force-action (VFA) model to develop an intuition of physics through reinforcement learning at scale. The Cambridge, Mass.-based company said that robots using its AI can pick a wide variety of objects outside the training distribution at a speed of roughly 1,500 operations per hour.

The same robots can screw in a light bulb and insert wires, Eka asserted.

Robots shouldn’t just mimic humans, says Eka Robotics

Eka Robotics said it is targeting dexterous manipulation. The company said that for robots to handle complicated work, they need the versatility to handle changing conditions and the performance to deliver useful work every day.

Eka also said it believes that robots should master physics, not mimic human data, to be truly general-purpose. This would allow the robot to build “intuition” for tasks the same way a human can by jointly reasoning about vision and forces.

The company uses simulation learning, and it said its VFA model is demonstrating that the typical sim-to-real barrier is falling. In simulation, the company can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes, varying objects, environments, and physical conditions.

Eka claimed that transferring this learning to the real world unlocks a scalable, performant, and capital-efficient path to a foundation model for manipulation. “Reinforcement learning at scale buys performance, and breadth of experience buys generality,” it said.

Investors seek to level up dexterous manipulation

Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and F-Prime, a venture capital fund affiliated with FMR LLC, the parent company of Fidelity Investments, led the round.

“Eka’s Vision-Force-Action model is the first approach I’ve seen that truly solves manipulation with the generality and throughput needed for deployments,” stated Raghu Raghuram, a general partner at a16z. “This team has the ideal DNA to push the frontier of robotics research while scaling commercial operations.”

Eka Robotics’ Series A included continued support from the lead investors in its seed round, Obvious Ventures and E14 Fund. Other funding came from MFV Partners, Bison Ventures, Glasswing Ventures, Samsung Next, and several Fortune 500 strategics.

“From the factory floor, a robot’s value comes down to two things: its success rate and its speed over thousands of repetitions,” said Shyam Kamadolli, a managing director at Fine Structure Ventures. “Early on, I recognized that current approaches to generalization simply won’t get us there. Achieving the next level of performance requires a deep understanding of physics and, crucially, breaking free from our dependence on human demonstrations.”

“Eka’s VFA model, trained through simulation and reinforcement learning, achieves this for the hardest problem in robotics, dexterous manipulation, in a way no other company has,” he added. “I truly believe Eka’s approach is the only one that will hold up in real-world deployments of complex tasks.”

item.title: Webinar to discuss how the FCC robotics ruling affects automation buyers
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Industry leaders will discuss what robotics buyers should know about the recent FCC restriction on certain connected systems.

The post Webinar to discuss how the FCC robotics ruling affects automation buyers appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Vecna Robotics makes its systems in the U.S. and is not directly affected by the FCC ruling. Credit: Eugene Demaitre

In July, the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, said it had determined that certain foreign-made advanced robots pose a cybersecurity and competitive risk to the U.S. It has restricted imports of new models of advanced robotic devices, including mobile robots and legged robots.

What should companies considering purchases of such robots do? What are some of the concerns around design, deployment, and ongoing support?

Leaders from Vecna Robotics, Locus Robotics, and the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) will discuss the practical implications of the commission‘s determination in a free webinar at 2:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. The panelists will examine how connected systems differ from traditional automation.

Webinar attendees can also learn how companies can evaluate the long-term supportability of their robotics investments. They will hear perspectives on strengthening supply chains, questions buyers should be asking their technology providers, and what the changing landscape could mean for the U.S. robotics industry.

Register now to learn about FCC policy implications

The webinar will also help attendees:

  • Identify what types of robots and companies are affected by the FCC action
  • Understand the intent behind the restriction and other U.S. policies under consideration, such as tariffs
  • Build acquisition, implementation, and service strategies for resilience
  • Track how the robotics ecosystem is reacting to U.S. and competitive challenges
  • Be aware of standards efforts in addition to regulatory changes
  • Look at long-term trends in automation

Register now to attend this webinar, which is sponsored by Vecna Robotics. The panelists will answer questions during the live broadcast, which will be available on demand afterwards to registrants.

About the webinar panelists

Karl Iagnemma is CEO of material handling systems provider Vecna Robotics Inc. He holds a Ph.D. from MIT and was director of the MIT Robotic Mobility Group.

Iagnemma previously founded nuTonomy, the world’s first venture-backed driverless car software business, which was acquired by Aptiv for $450 million. Under his leadership, nuTonomy was spun out into Motional, a $4 billion joint venture with Hyundai Motor Co.

Karl brings a wealth of experience in scaling robotics companies from research through commercialization to Vecna.

Rick Faulk is CEO of warehouse automation supplier Locus Robotics Corp. He leads its executive team with more than 30 years of experience in executive management, sales, and marketing for some of the world’s most successful technology companies, such as Cisco, Intronis, j2 Global, WebEx, Intranets.com, Barracuda Networks, Lotus Development, Mzinga, and PictureTel.

Faulk leads Locus Robotics’ executive team and is responsible for the overall strategy and execution at the company. Rick currently sits on various boards and is an advisor to multiple companies, including Retrocausal, Arccos, Cybernetix Ventures, and Leading Edge Ventures. Past board positions include Yodle, Virtual Computer, Bidding for Good, Skill Survey, Influitive, Ntirety, Blue Raven, and Centive.

Aaron Prather is director of market intelligence at the Association for Advancing Automation. He leads the organization’s efforts to transform raw market data into actionable insights that support the strategic decision-making of executive leadership.

With a focus on the robotics and automation sector, Prather helps build a coherent understanding of industry trends, enabling confident and informed business strategies.

With over two decades of experience, Aaron has contributed to the advancement of automation, robotics, and operations management through roles emphasizing R&D, standardization, and strategic planning.

Eugene Demaitre, moderator, is editorial director for robotics at Arrowfly (formerly WTWH Media), which produces The Robot Report, Automated Warehouse, the Robotics Summit & Expo, and RoboBusiness (now Robotics Summit West).

Prior to working for Arrowfly, he was an editor at BNA (now part of Bloomberg), Computerworld, TechTarget, and Robotics Business Review. Demaitre has participated in conferences worldwide, as well as spoken in numerous webinars and podcasts. He recently led a discussion on reshoring at RoboBusiness 2026.

Gene is always interested in learning more about robotics. He has a master’s from the George Washington University and lives in the Boston area.

The post Webinar to discuss how the FCC robotics ruling affects automation buyers appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Generative Bionics to launch Physical AI Data Factory in Italy
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Generative Bionics says it hopes to advance European robotics sovereignty by ensuring that humanoid data is are generated on the continent. 

The post Generative Bionics to launch Physical AI Data Factory in Italy appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The first Data Factory hub is set to become one of Europe’s largest physical AI training facilities for humanoid robots. | Source: Generative Bionics

Generative Bionics this week announced plans to build a proprietary, multi-site “Physical AI Data Factory” in Italy. The company said the new 5,000-sq.-m (53,819.5-sq.-ft.) hub will help move humanoid robotics from laboratory demonstrations to reliable industrial deployment.

In addition, Generative Bionics said it hopes to advance European humanoid sovereignty, ensuring that the data, models, and know-how behind Europe’s industrial humanoids are generated, trained and validated on the continent.

“The value that Europe has right now is within its industry, and we have to extract physical AI data in order to train our own models,” Daniele Pucci, the CEO of Generative Bionics, told The Robot Report. “This is a competitive advantage that Europe right now has, because of the automation that we have been putting in place over the last 40 years.”

Generative Bionics said the new facility will be operational by the fourth quarter of 2027. The Genoa, Italy-based company plans to eventually open a second facility elsewhere in Europe and a third serving global markets. Together, the three facilities will reproduce real industrial environments, generate high-fidelity physical data, and connect that data with large-scale simulation.

Building on their strategic technology collaboration, Advanced Micro Devices Inc. will be Generative Bionics’ AI infrastructure partner, and the Physical AI Data Factory network will be powered by AMD Helios. Its rack-scale architecture will provide the compute foundation to process physical and synthetic data, train physical AI models, and run thousands of digital-twin scenario variations in parallel.

Data Factory to test GENE.01 in a range of industries

The Physical AI Data Factory will connect real-world robot operations, simulation and AI development in a continuous real-to-sim-to-real cycle, said Generative Bionics. The company said this will allow it to configure and validate its GENE.01 humanoid robot for specific industrial environments before customer deployment, then feed data from deployed fleets into future training cycles.

Industrial humanoids must learn from the conditions they will encounter at work, noted the Generative Bionics. This requires data that captures contact, force, motion, proximity, temperature, task constraints, and human interaction in realistic operating settings. For GENE.01, the dataset will include vision and motion data as well as signals captured through its full-body multimodal skin.

“A robot is not only vision and is not only language,” said Pucci. “It is position, velocity, acceleration, temperature, and contact forces, so there is a large variety of data that you have to take into account.”

The Data Factory will reproduce environments selected with industrial partners and allow fleets of GENE.01 robots to perform tasks continuously in real-world conditions. These operations will generate high-fidelity physical data for training world action models (WAM) and validating the complete robot system, including perception, control, safety behavior, and task execution, before deployment at customer sites.

Each physical environment and robot configuration will also be recreated as a digital twin. The same tasks can then be repeated across thousands of variations in layout, objects, materials, operating conditions, and failure modes that would be impractical to reproduce physically. Models trained and tested in simulation will be deployed back to the robots for validation, while data from physical operations will feed the next training cycle.

Generative Bionics wants to help find robot ‘ChatGPT moment’

Large language models (LLMs) learn from vast amounts of information available online, noted Generative Bionics. Humanoid robots have no comparable source of data on how to act in the physical world.

The Physical AI Data Factory will create such a source by collecting data as GENE.01 performs industrial tasks and expanding those experiences through digital-twins running on AMD compute.

“We have the ambition of being the European champion in physical AI, and even robotics, designed to scale globally,” said Pucci. “That’s our clear positioning, and for this, we are taking a close look at the supply chain that can supply our future manufacturing.”

“Manufacturing here is divided into three levels: the manufacturing of data, the manufacturing of robots, and the manufacturing of models,” she continued. Pucci said if Europe wants to achieve sovereignty in this area, it needs to invest in all three.

Right now, humanoid robots from China have been garnering a lot of attention with flashy demos and large funding rounds. But, Pucci, notes that this doesn’t mean the country is necessarily ahead of Europe.

“I want to be crystal clear about this. Many of the Chinese robots that are out there are simply not certified to enter industrial settings,” Pucci said. “The narrative that the Chinese solved as the issues is very far from reality.”

“Right now, we believe that many of the existing solutions are basically for entertainment, and this is a market segment that we respect,” she added. “But, Generative Bionics is taking the issue of safety and certification very seriously because we want to go B2B first.”

GENE.01 can be customized for specific applications

Generative Bionics claimed that a few things separate its platform from the average humanoid robot. To start, GENE.01 features full-body tactile sensing.

“It comes naturally to give the humanoid robots the sense of touch, because humanoid robots have to perceive people not only while talking, but also while interacting with them physically,” Pucci said. “That’s why GENE was given this unique multimodal scheme, which can perceive not only the sense of touch but also the sense of proximity.”

Generative Bionics also plans to offer GENE.01 as a base platform that can be customized for different industries.

“We have a clear view that humanoid robots cannot be used for anything that comes to your mind, because a humanoid robot welding in a shipyard cannot be the same as a humanoid robot in healthcare,” noted Pucci. “There is a fundamental difference in the development cycle.”

The company has three levels of customization. “The first one is the AI, because a robot moving boxes does not need the same AI of a robot in healthcare,” said Pucci. “The second is the exterior design. In the shipyard, you have to be resistant against high temperatures, sparks, and powders. The third is the hands and the feet.”

“This is really scalable at the manufacturing level, because you have a common platform, and then you can customize at the end the so-called end of lines at these three levels,” she continued. “This is basically the same approach that you have in automotive.”

Generative Bionics is building on more than 20 years of research, development, and prototyping of humanoids at the Italian Institute of Technology (IIT). The company spun out of IIT in 2024, and IIT has granted it exclusive licenses to key technologies.

item.title: Dream Labs raises $90M and launches Dream API
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Dream Labs says its Dream-1 AI model works across robots from different manufacturers and will allow robots to transfer their learning.

The post Dream Labs raises $90M and launches Dream API appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Dream Labs said its models learn how the physical world works from video and can control new robots without any data. | Source: Dream Labs

More brains are coming for robots. Dream Labs this week said it has raised $90 million in seed funding. The company also launched Dream API, a publicly available application programming interface to turn a robot’s camera feed and a plain-English instructions into motor commands, even for robots it has never seen before.

Factories worldwide run a record 5 million industrial robots, yet nearly every one is programmed for a single task, and most cannot transfer what they have learned to other machines, noted Dream Labs. Low-cost robots now sell for a few thousand dollars but ship with no built-in intelligence. Teaching one robot one task can take specialists months, and a new task or new hardware often means starting from zero, according to the San Francisco startup.

Dream Labs said its Dream-1 flagship model works across robots from different manufacturers. Trained on video of people performing everyday tasks, it can predict what will happen next and determine the robot’s resulting action. Because it learns from video rather than from a single machine, its capabilities transfer across hardware, Dream Labs claimed.

The company said Dream-1 can control any robot “out of the box” with grippers and zero-shot learning.

“The hardware is ready. What’s been missing is a brain any robot can use,” stated Joel Jang, co-founder and CEO of Dream Labs. “When you get into a rental car, you don’t relearn how to drive. You find the controls, and your past driving experience does the rest.”

“Dream-1 approaches a new robot the same way, so a new robot can do useful work in minutes, not months,” he added. “And instead of edited demos, we’re giving people a working model they can test themselves, mistakes included.”

B Capital and Kindred Ventures led the round. It also included participation from A.Capital, Unusual Ventures, SV Angel, Wing VC, Scribble VC, and Adrian Aoun, among others.

Inside Dream Labs’ product portfolio

Developers and robot enthusiasts can start using Dream Labs’ AI products today. The company said Dream API translates visual inputs and natural language prompts directly into robot actions.

Developers can sign up, connect any robots with grippers, and the robot will carry out the task. Dream Labs runs its models in data centers around the world, so robots respond quickly wherever they are.

The company also offers fine-tuning as a service. For unsupported hardware or new capabilities, developers and robot makers can submit a small batch of demonstration data to receive a tailored model within hours.

Developers also have access to Dream Labs’ robot playground. Anyone with a browser can type commands to a robot in Dream Labs’ San Francisco office and watch it respond live and unedited, no robot purchase required.

“A capable robot arm has gone from the price of a luxury car to the price of a high-end laptop. What it needs now is intelligence,” said Daisy Cai, general partner at B Capital. “This team did some of the defining work in robot learning at NVIDIA. Now anyone with an API key can build on it.”

Startup works with more than 20 hardware partners

Dream Labs supports robots today that cost between about $2,000 and $10,000. Dream-1 needs no extra data to control a two-armed robot with parallel grippers.

For its over 20 hardware partners, Dream Labs said it goes beyond that baseline, refining the model for each robot so it performs at its best. Dream-1 currently handles tabletop tasks such as picking and placing objects and folding laundry, with support for wheeled mobile robots and dexterous hands to follow.

The company said it plans use the new funding primarily for compute as it expands the tasks and robots Dream-1 can handle, and scales to support more users.

“Our customers buy our robots to build things, and the hardest part has always been getting them to do actual work,” said Ryan Chan, co-founder and CEO of MakerMods, which sells $2,000 bimanual robot arms. “With Dream-1, our robot was up and running in a few minutes and attempting tasks we never programmed. We can focus on building better hardware, and our customers get intelligence that keeps improving.”

item.title: AGCO to deploy Agility Digit humanoid in Kansas factory
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
The Agility pilot, which is expected to begin in 2027, will begin at an AGCO production facility for agricultural equipment.

The post AGCO to deploy Agility Digit humanoid in Kansas factory appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The news comes as Agility inches closer to its IPO via SPAC and after it announced the latest version of Digit. | Source: Agility Robotics

AGCO and Agility Robotics have signed a commercial agreement to deploy Agility’s Digit humanoid in AGCO’s manufacturing facility. The U.S. pilot, expected to begin in 2027, will support AGCO’s efforts to create more flexible, intelligent factories, beginning at its production site in Hesston, Kan.

“This strategic relationship views humanoid robotics and AI as essential ’teammates‘ in building flexible, intelligent factories,” stated Thomas Enghof, director of manufacturing technology at AGCO. “They unlock automation in complex, human-centric workflows, augmenting human capabilities by absorbing repetitive, strenuous or hazardous tasks. By pairing human ingenuity with robust robotic engineering and strict safety governance, we create resilient manufacturing systems that empower the workforce and deliver measurable business value.”

AGCO said it is a global leader in agricultural machinery and precision agriculture technologies. The Duluth, Ga.-based company‘s brands include Fendt, Massey Ferguson, PTx, and Valtra. AGCO said its high-performance equipment and smart farming systems, including brand-agnostic retrofit technologies and autonomous offerings, “empower farmers to drive productivity while sustainably feeding the world.”

AGCO joins a growing list of Digit deployments

Digit uses AI to continuously learn and adapt to evolving workflows, enabling greater operational flexibility and improved productivity, according to Agility. When paired with the Agility Arc cloud-based platform for deploying and managing robot fleets, companies can rapidly integrate automation into essential operations without requiring extensive infrastructure changes or costly facility upgrades, it added.

AGCO joins a growing number of global leading companies deploying Agility’s humanoid robots, including Toyota, GXO Logistics, and Schaeffler.

“We’re excited to work alongside AGCO as they continue to lead the way in agricultural innovation,” said Daniel Diez, chief business officer of Agility. “By introducing Agility’s Digit humanoid robots into AGCO’s operations, we have an opportunity to strengthen manufacturing processes, support employees in demanding tasks, and demonstrate how advanced robotics can create measurable impact across modern production environments.”

Submit your innovation now!

Agility is on the move

Agility said its humanoid robot will initially support key assembly and production operations including sorting and stacking parts sorting, as well as intelligent placement of totes for storage. The physical AI company asserted that Digit will enhance ergonomic safety, improve operational efficiency, and empower employees to focus on higher-value, skill-driven work that advances innovation and productivity.

It has been a busy time for Agility Robotics. Last month, the company unveiled the latest version of its robot, Digit 5. The latest version of Digit includes new legs, upgraded batteries, and a more comprehensive safety architecture. The Salem, Ore.-based company also recently confirmed that it is exploring building wheeled robots for its customers.

Agility is preparing to become a public company through its previously announced merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI. The business combination is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, after which the combined company will operate as Agility Robotics and is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “AGLT.”

item.title: A guide to Day 2 of RoboBusiness 2026
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Day 2 of RoboBusiness 2026, the 20th anniversary of the event, will include interesting keynotes around humanoids and social robots.

The post A guide to Day 2 of RoboBusiness 2026 appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Deepu Talla, NVIDIA’s VP of robotics and edge AI, gave the opening talk at RoboBusiness 2025.

RoboBusiness 2026 will come to an end today. After a packed first day of the 20th anniversary show, here is everything you need to know about Day 2.

The second day of RoboBusiness will start at 9:30 a.m. PT with the “State of Humanoids” panel. During this keynote, industry leaders will explore the capabilities humanoids are delivering today, the technical and operational challenges that remain, and the lessons emerging from early industrial implementations. All keynotes will take place in the theater on the second floor.

This panel will include insights from Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer of Agility Robotics; Parker Conroy, the head of product management at Apptronik; Michael Patrick Perry, head of commercial strategy at Persona AI; Aadeel Akhtar, the founder and CEO of PSYONIC. Mike Oitzman, senior editor at The Robot Report, will host the panel.

The Exhibitor Hall will open at 10:00 a.m. and stay open until 3:00 p.m. There, attendees can find interesting robotics demos and the Startup Alley.

We’ll be closing RoboBusiness 2026 with a final keynote talk at 3:00 p.m. Morgan Pope, the director of companionship at Familiar Machines & Magic, will lead a session on how the startup is creating robotic characters.

Registration for the show is available on site.

Morning breakout session schedule

Breakout sessions will start after the morning keynote and a short networking break. RoboBusiness 2026 sessions starting at 10:45 a.m. include:

  • Egocentric Robot Learning: Teaching Robots Through Human Experience: Ted Larson, co-founder and CEO of OLogic, will explore the foundations of egocentric robot learning, the technical challenges involved in building these systems, and their implications for the future of commercial robotics. His talk will be in Room 203.
  • China’s Physical AI Ecosystem in 2026: Competitor, Supplier, Benchmark: Georg Stieler, managing director for Asia at Stieler Technology, will share the latest insights from his company’s work on the ground in China and put them into global perspective. The session will be in Room 207.
  • An Introduction to Robotic Tools for Overhead Power Line Operations: Trevor Anderson, the chief strategy officer at FulcrumAir, will examine mobilization, installation precision, live-line capabilities and opportunities to complete work without helicopters or required outages. The talk will take place in Room 209/210.
  • Precision, Power, Perception: Enabling Next-Gen Humanoid Actuation: Jordan Grotz, senior robotics systems engineer at Allegro MicroSystems, will dissect the critical technological advancements that are making next-generation robotic actuation possible. He will speak in Room 206.
  • Why Physical AI Fails in the Real World: This panel will include insights from SK Gupta, co-founder and chief scientist of GrayMatter Robotics; Brian Geisel, founder and CEO of Geisel Software & Symage; and Sparsh Gautam, a computer vision engineer at Tesla. They will discuss how teams are addressing challenges across perception, decision-making, and manipulation to create robots that can operate safely and predictably outside the lab. The session will be in Room 204.

Sessions starting at 11:45 a.m. include:

  • Building Physical AI that Scales: Dermot O’Driscoll, vice president of go-to-market physical AI at Arm, will examine key compute principles behind trusted physical AI, including how intelligence is distributed across cloud and edge compute and the coordination of learned and deterministic behaviors. He will also explain how developers can design systems that remain adaptable, reliable, and safe as they scale to production. The talk will be in Room 203.
  • Reshoring With Robots: A Policy Discussion: This panel discussion will include insights from Ellie Sakhaee, an AI policy manager at Google; Dr. Henrik I Christensen, a distinguished professor of computer science at UC San Diego; Brendan Schulman, vice president of policy and government relations at Boston Dynamics; and Michael Bearman, the chief legal and safety officer at Vecna Robotics. The group will examine the need for a national robotics strategy and debate industrial priorities. Eugene Demaitre, editorial director for The Robot Report, will moderate this session in Room 207.
  • SparkE-B: Building a Robot for Safer Electrical Work:  Yakov Bobrov, co-founder and chief technology officer of Hardhat Robotics, will explore the challenges of deploying robots in dynamic construction environments, the engineering behind safety-critical robotic systems, and how AI-enabled autonomy could help skilled tradespeople dramatically increase productivity. The talk will take place in Room 209/210.
  • The Dexterous Hand: Delivering Force and Signal via Synthetic Tendons: Jim Hotary, VP of technology at Maeden Innovation, will examine key engineering challenges including fatigue life, creep, abrasion resistance, friction management, routing constraints, and reliability under millions of flex cycles. His session will be in Room 206.
  • Human-Robot Interaction: Bridging Academia and Industry: Fraz Yousuf, a senior robotics application engineer at Eli Lilly, will share what they learned running HRI field studies with manufacturing and warehouse operators around live AGVs, some early findings of people’s perception of robots on the manufacturing floor and the playbook they built to make the partnership repeatable. This talk will take place in Room 204.

RoboBusiness 2026 features more afternoon sessions

Breakout sessions starting at 2:00 p.m. include:

  • Real-Time Robot Troubleshooting with AI Agents and MCP: Rohit John Varghese, the director of systems engineering and product at Contoro Robotics, will give an introduction to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and then show examples on a real industrial robot deployed in a warehouse. The talk will be in Room 206.
  • The ROI of Reality: Investing in the Physical AI Frontier: David Sokolic, a partner at Toyota Ventures, will break down what it takes to build, fund, and scale intelligent physical systems. The presentation will be in Room 207.
  • How to Pick Winners in Robotics: What Programs and IP to Pursue and Why: Spencer Krause, the president and CEO of SKA Robotics, go through some of the methodologies that Krause uses when evaluating the viability of a business case for robotics and also whether or not to accept a partner engagement. It will be in Room 209/210.
  • Intelligence Behind Warehouse Robotics: Scaling Operations with AI & Software: Jingwei Tan, a senior system consultant at Geek+, and Joe Kraft, the director of system consulting at Geek+, will examine how software, not just hardware, enables organizations to expand from a single automated workflow to enterprise-scale warehouse operations, while reducing complexity, improving resource utilization, and accelerating ROI. This RoboBusiness 2026 talk will take place in Room 204.

item.title: Reservoir launches new agricultural robotics incubator for Washington growers
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Reservoir hopes to put agricultural robotics startups to work in the orchards, vineyards and berry fields alongside researchers and growers.

The post Reservoir launches new agricultural robotics incubator for Washington growers appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Reservoir opened Reservoir Farms – Salinas, its flagship innovation hub. | Source: Reservoir

Reservoir, Washington State University’s Prosser Irrigated Agriculture Research and Extension Center (IAREC), the Washington Tree Fruit Research Commission (WTFRC), and the Tri-City Development Council (TRIDEC) today announced a new agricultural robotics incubator for Washington growers. 

The site will put agricultural robotics startups to work in the state’s orchards, vineyards and berry fields alongside researchers and growers.

The announcement comes as Washington growers face rising labor costs and a shrinking workforce for some of the hardest crops in the world to automate. These include apples, cherries, pears, blueberries, wine grapes, and hops.

Reservoir is an agricultural innovation center and venture capital fund. The organization is focused on helping agtech startups succeed where agriculture happens, in the field.

Reservoir started its innovation center in the Salinas Valley. It hopes to expand to other key regions across California and the American West. Reservoir VC backs startups solving real problems in high-value crops and the rugged physical AI stack.

More about Reservoir’s innovation center

Earlier this year, the company officially opened Reservoir Farms – Salinas, its flagship on-farm innovation hub for specialty crops. The new site features multiple innovation barns and 24 acres of dedicated commercial test fields. This creates the most concentrated ecosystem of technology leaders, growers, and startups anywhere in agriculture to rapidly scale solutions for global food production challenges.

More than 300 growers, agricultural leaders, federal and state officials, community partners, investors and media attended the grand opening of Salinas site.

“From our early days, Reservoir listened intently to partners to understand where innovation in agriculture was stuck,” said Danny Bernstein, founder and CEO of Reservoir. “Once our vision to create an on-farm innovation center was clear, we worked relentlessly with partners across the industry to bring the energy, focus and skills necessary to manifest the space and people necessary to make this a reality. With the doors open, the focus turns to execution and impact – in the form of real-world solutions for growers, upskilled jobs for rural communities, and a more secure food supply for American consumers.”

Last summer, Reservoir announced plans to expand its on-farm innovation center model across California, Arizona, and other major growing regions. Each hub will be anchored by leading academic and research and developmnt institutions.

As part of this multi-region strategy, Reservoir invited startups to run pilots over the winter months at the University of Arizona’s Yuma Agricultural Center. The startups gained the opportunity to test technologies in commercial desert vegetable production.

In August, Reservoir announced a $10 million, three-year R&D partnership with John Deere. The partnership aims to accelerate real-world development and commercialization of rugged AI technologies for high-value crop agriculture. It builds on a relationship that began when Reservoir was founded in 2024.

Deere said the partnership with Reservoir reflects its “commitment to an innovation ecosystem that moves faster from prototype to grower impact.”

item.title: RoboBusiness rebrands as Robotics Summit & Expo West
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
Robotics Summit & Expo West sharpens focus on deploying robotics and AI in the real world, complementing the East Coast flagship event.

The post RoboBusiness rebrands as Robotics Summit & Expo West appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Arrowfly, an award-winning B2B media and marketing company, today announced that RoboBusiness, the leading robotics industry event for the past 20 years, is being rebranded as Robotics Summit & Expo West, a conference and expo dedicated to the design, deployment, and scaling of commercial robots and businesses. The first event under the new name will be in October 2027 in Santa Clara, Calif.

The timing reflects how the industry has matured. Many robotics companies have moved past the prototype stage, shipping real products into factories, warehouses, and other sites. The questions that define their work are no longer only technical. They are about design for manufacturing, bringing products to market, implementation, managing growing fleets, and providing service and support. Robotics Summit & Expo West will help industry professionals meet increasing demand for intelligent systems across sectors.

“The robotics industry has matured, and the hardest problems have grown with it,” said Steve Crowe, executive editor of The Robot Report and chair of the Robotics Summit. “For 20 years, RoboBusiness brought this community together. Robotics Summit & Expo West will serve that community by sharing lessons from industry leaders on how to move from a pilot that works to a product deployed across multiple sites and building a business that can support it.”

Robotics Summit & Expo West is organized around the questions that define the post-prototype stage of a robotics company:

Deployment at scale: What changes when a robot moves from a controlled pilot to multiple live sites, including integration, fleet management, remote monitoring, and autonomous operations in increasingly unstructured environments.

Go-to-market and commercial strategy: How robotics companies are responding to market demand and structuring pricing, sales, and channel strategies for products that combine hardware, software, and services.

Field data and product decisions: How real-world performance data flows back into product iteration and AI model evolution. Ongoing service and support, whether directly or through partners, is also key to demonstrating a return on investment.

Investment and growth: How investors evaluate robotics companies, and how founding teams can build businesses that last.

The conference program includes keynotes with industry and thought leaders, sessions focused on the latest technical and business topics, insightful panel discussions, and a curated expo floor. Attendees can learn from the founders, operators, and investors who are shaping the future of robotics.

One mission. Two conversations

The rebrand clarifies Arrowfly’s robotics event portfolio. Robotics Summit & Expo Boston (June 2–3, 2027, John B. Hynes Convention Center), the flagship East Coast show, focuses on the core technical and engineering challenges of building robotic systems. Robotics Summit & Expo West focuses on scaling the product and the company behind it. Together, the two events serve the full lifecycle of designing, building, and bringing a robotics product to market.

“Deployment does not end the development process. It changes who is asking the questions,” said Amanda Buehner, senior vice president of sales & strategy, engineering, at Arrowfly. “The engineer designing a new mobile robot and the operations leader managing robots across a warehouse network are both essential to this industry. They need different conversations. That is what the Robotics Summit lineup now provides.”

Robotics hardware, software, and solution providers looking to reach the engineers, product leaders, and executives scaling robotics can learn about sponsorship and exhibit opportunities by contacting Arrowfly’s robotics team.

About Arrowfly

Arrowfly is a live and digital B2B destination serving professionals across the engineering, healthcare, food, retail, and hospitality sectors. Across 40+ brands, the company delivers trusted journalism, original content, live and digital events, video, and demand generation programs to the decisionmakers shaping their industries. Powered by Clara, Arrowfly’s proprietary performance platform, partners get real-time visibility into audience engagement, lead quality, and campaign ROI. The company is backed by an established reputation for editorial independence and credibility across the markets it serves. For more information, visit arrowfly.com.

Media Contact
Annie Wissner
VP of Marketing, Arrowfly
awissner@arrowfly.com

The post RoboBusiness rebrands as Robotics Summit & Expo West appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: 2027 TRR50 Robotics Innovation Awards open nominations
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
The TRR50 winners will be celebrated at an awards gala during the Robotics Summit & Expo, which will be held on June 2-3, 2027 in Boston.

The post 2027 TRR50 Robotics Innovation Awards open nominations appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Aaron Parness, director of applied sciences at Amazon Robotics, and Bhavana Chandrashekhar, the senior manager of applied science at Amazon Robotics, speaking at the 2026 RBR50 gala.

The Robot Report is seeking nominations for its 2026 TRR50 Robotics Innovation Awards. The RBR50 has recognized the most innovative organizations and robots since 2012, and this year we’re rebranding to The Robot Report 50 (TRR50). Here are the winners from 2026, 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022, and 2021.

Each year, The Robot Report selects the most interesting and important robotics innovations from around the world. The deadline for submissions is Friday, Jan. 5, 2027. Submit your nomination(s) below.

The TRR50 winners will be celebrated at an awards gala during the Robotics Summit & Expo, which will be held on June 2 and 3, 2027 in Boston. Some of the winners will also be demoing their robots on the Robotics Summit expo floor in the TRR50 Pavilion.

TRR50 Awards categories

To be eligible, all nominations must be for innovations that were initiated, released, or executed between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31, 2026. The TRR50 is looking for submissions in the following categories:

Startup of the Year: The nominee must be less than five years, and it must be already testing its innovation with customers. Last year, Physical Intelligence, which offers AI models that change how robots learn, earned the Startup of the Year award, and the year before, Mytra took home the honors.

Application of the Year: The winner will be a use case that has previously been difficult to automate and where robotics and automation have demonstrated a clear benefit over previous processes. Last year, Harvard University won for its wearable robot aids to help those struggling after a stroke or with ALS. The year before, TEPCO won for its work to remove radioactive fuel from Japan’s Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant.

Robot of the Year: The TRR50 awards are seeking a robot that is a game-changer in terms of technology innovation, use case, and industry influence. Amazon’s Vulcan robot won the award in 2026, and Robotaxi developer Waymo won in 2025.

Robots for Good: The TRR50 Robots for Good Award honors a robot that make a positive impact on society by addressing social challenges, improving quality of life or work, or promoting sustainability. Tatum Robotics won in 2026 for its robotic hand that enables tactile sign language communication. In 2025, Hello Robot’s Stretch 3 mobile manipulator won the inaugural Robots for Good Award.

Best use of AI: The TRR50 Best Use of AI Award will honor a real-world application for AI in robotics. This new category will highlight one use case that exemplifies how AI is changing robotics.

Products: This category honors new robots, enabling technologies, and research.

Business: This category honors major milestones, unique business models, and other initiatives positioning a company as a market leader.

Applications: The TRR50 will also recognize innovations that improve productivity, quality, and cost-effectiveness, as well as those that automate new tasks.

For any questions related to the 2027 TRR50 Robotics Innovation Awards, please contact Steve Crowe.

item.title: Avenda Health expands Unfold AI platform to support intraoperative prostate cancer care
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Surgery Mode in Unfold AI brings patient-specific 3D maps to give an enhanced view of cancer anatomy during robotic prostate procedures.

The post Avenda Health expands Unfold AI platform to support intraoperative prostate cancer care appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Unfold AI is designed to help physicians identify cancerous tissue. Source: Avenda Health

Prostate treatment has improved with robotics, and it could improve again soon with artificial intelligence. Avenda Health today announced Surgery Mode, a new suit of interoperative features for its Unfold AI offering. The multimodal AI-powered prostate cancer mapping platform is designed to reveal the true size and extent of disease to help physicians make better informed treatment decisions.

“Our goal with Unfold AI has always been to provide more clinical clarity throughout every stage of a patient’s cancer journey,” stated Shyam Natarajan, Ph.D., co-founder and CEO of Avenda Health.

“Whether a physician is counseling a newly diagnosed patient, planning a targeted radiation oncology treatment, or performing a complex radical prostatectomy, having an accurate 3D map of the disease is transformative,” he added. “These new surgical enhancements empower physicians with the visual confidence needed to achieve optimal cancer control while protecting patient quality of life during complex procedures.”

Founded in 2017, Avenda Health said it is creating a more personalized future of prostate cancer care. With deep learning, the Culver City, Calif.-based company‘s software maps a patient’s cancer in 3D, giving physicians precise information and the confidence to make care decisions. Avenda said it aims to improve outcomes, preserve quality of life, and create a new standard of prostate cancer care.

Avenda Health bases Surgery Mode on research

Avenda Health said it designed Surgery Mode to enhance how surgeons use 3D AI mapping during non-robotic and robotic surgeries, alongside new tools to simplify patient case management and physician workflows.

The launch builds on peer-reviewed research predicting that Unfold AI could cut positive surgical margins in half, substantially reducing cancer recurrence. In the study, the system outperformed MRI and other modalities in assessing whether cancer had spread beyond the prostate, assisting surgeons in making nerve-sparing decisions.

In Surgery Mode, physicians can now access enlarged 3D views for clearer visualization, adjust the cancer estimation map to match the camera angle on the surgical console, review underlying MRI slices during the procedure, and access capsule risk scores from within a dedicated surgical view.

Avenda Health claimed that Unfold AI is the only platform implementing multimodal AI to analyze a patient’s MRI, biopsy, pathology, and PSA together. It produces a personalized 3D map of the cancer’s extent to provide surgeons with more precise visualization of tumor boundaries.

While Unfold AI has served as a decision-support tool during preoperative consultations, the latest expansion gives surgeons an enhanced version of these maps during prostate procedures. The suite of improved workflow tools also gives physicians and staff greater visibility into the status of each patient case.

Submit your innovation now!

Key features

  • Aligned Capsule Risk Score mapping: The Capsule Risk Score overlay now automatically flips its left/right visual orientation to mirror the surgical camera view, giving surgeons immediate, color-coded risk feedback by quadrant to guide precise nerve-sparing decisions in real time.
  • Redesigned patient list and case filters: Improved patient organization and updated case status labels let users search for cases in progress, add new patients, and filter by status to see where each case stands at a glance.
  • Improved administrative control: New built-in tools let staff verify insurance approvals and confirm administrative steps are complete before 3D map generation.
  • Streamlined case management: Care teams can now add and view patient notes directly from the patient list and update the assigned physician on a patient report.

Unfold AI helps doctors identify tumor extent

Avenda Health said the expanded features extend Unfold AI’s reach across the prostate cancer care pathway, including active surveillance, focal therapy, surgical interventions, and radiotherapy. Its interactive 3D maps serve as a visual guide for patient counseling and decision support, helping patients and physicians confidently select their treatment path.

Now, with Surgery Mode, the same patient-specific mapping technology can be used to provide clear visual boundaries in the operating room, actively guiding surgical procedures such as robotic prostatectomies.

Unfold AI predicts the cancer’s spread into nearby anatomy with 92% accuracy, compared with 52% using MRI alone. That spatial clarity is central to helping surgeons determine whether a nerve-sparing or non-nerve-sparing surgery should be performed.

Avenda noted that additional research demonstrated that Unfold AI improves physician identification of tumor extent, increasing sensitivity from 37% to 97%. By expanding Unfold AI from preoperative decision support into the operating room, the company said it is developing more precise views of prostate cancer that can support physicians across different stages of care.

item.title: A guide to Day 1 of RoboBusiness 2026
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
We've compiled a schedule for everything happening on the first day of RoboBusiness 2026 in Santa Clara, Calif.

The post A guide to Day 1 of RoboBusiness 2026 appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Today marks the start of RoboBusiness 2026! This year, we’ll be celebrating the 20th anniversary of RoboBusiness with the community that made it possible and looking ahead to more years of collaboration and growth.

The event will start at the Santa Clara Convention Center at 9:15 a.m. PT with the opening keynote, “The Next 20 Years of Robotics.” As RoboBusiness marks its 20th anniversary, industry leaders will reflect on the breakthroughs that defined the past two decades and explore the technologies, markets, opportunities, and challenges that will shape the next 20 years. This year, all keynotes will take place in the theatre on the second floor.

This talk will include Rodney Brooks, the co-founder and CTO of Robust AI; Jonathan Hurst, the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics; and Ken Goldberg, the William S. Floyd Jr Distinguished Chair in Engineering at UC Berkeley.

At 10:00 a.m., the RoboBusiness show floor will open. There, attendees can find interesting robotics demonstrations, the Engineering Theater, and the Startup Alley.

The day will close with another keynote talk, “Beyond the Demo: AI in Production Robotics” at 4:30 p.m. It will include insights from Bhavana Chandrashekhar, the senior manager of applied science at Amazon Robotics; James Davidson, the chief AI officer at Teradyne Robotics; Ali Raja, vice president of data centers at ABB Robotics; Ram Devarajulu, vice president of deep tech innovations at Cambridge Consultants; and Jon Battles, the vice president of technology strategy at Cobot.

After the final keynote, head back to the exhibitor hall for the Networking Reception presented by Harmonic Drive. The reception will include drinks, light appetizers, and time to connect with other RoboBusiness 2026 attendees and speakers.

Registration for the show is available on site.

Morning breakout session schedule

RoboBusiness 2026 breakout sessions will start at 10:30 a.m. upstairs from the show floor. They include:

  • Designing Data Programs for Humans, Not Robots: Aaron Bromberg, the head of robotics and physical AI at Instawork, will explain what it takes to capture usable data from real workers on real shifts, and what he has learned putting camera systems into commercial environments at scale. This talk will be in Room 209/210.
  • Startup Bootcamp Part 1: The Basics to Best Practices: Colleen Anderson, the director of community and events at MassRobotics; John Lanza and Jennifer Audeh, partners at Foley Hoag; and Brooke Fritz, a partner of tech transactions at Foley Hoag, will provide best practices for robotics startups. The session will be in Room 207.
  • Designing the Robotics Ecosystem for Outdoor Autonomy: In this session, Mel Torrie, the CEO of Autonomous Solutions Inc., will explain why the intersection of autonomous vehicles and advanced robotics will further revolutionize field deployments. It will take place in Room 206.
  • The Humanoid Bill of Materials: De-Risking the Multi-Billion Dollar Bottleneck: Michelle Sun, the founder of Core Matter Labs, will strip away the marketing hype to expose the stark economic and geopolitical realities of the physical AI supply chain. The session will be in Room 203.
  • Integrated Drive Actuator Design: Combining Gearheads, Motor, Drive and Sensors for Smarter Motion: Marcel Almonte, a mechatronics applications engineer at Harmonic Drive, will teach attendees how integrated actuators can reduce engineering effort by simplifying system integration, minimizing cabling complexity, shortening testing and commissioning, and accelerating time to market. His session will start at 10:30 a.m.

Sessions starting at 11:30 a.m. include:

  • Why Food is Physical AI’s Hardest Problem & Most Promising Catalyst: Rajat Bhageria, the founder and CEO of Chef Robotics, will explore what makes food such a demanding benchmark for physical AI. This session will be in Room 209/210.
  • Startup Boot Camp Part 2: Challenges & Best Practices for Working with Corporate Partners: Joyce Sidopoulos, co-founder and chief of operations at MassRobotics; Ben Waters, co-founder and CEO of WiBotic; and Colm Prendergast, senior director and head of the Emerging Tech Hub at Analog Devices, will provide actionable strategies for successfully collaborating with corporate partners. The session will take place in Room 207.
  • Deployment Over Demos: Building Risk-Aware Foundation Models for Safety-Critical Environments: In this fireside chat, Andrey Konchenko, the head of product at FieldAI, will describe how a physics-first foundation model designed specifically for physical AI can address long-standing autonomy challenges in robotics. This talk will be in Room 206.
  • A Joint-by-Joint Guide to Humanoid Motion: Yoshi Umeno, the global director of business development for robotics at Kollmorgen, and Reginald Duffus, the supervisor of application engineering at Kollmorgen, will provide a practical framework for evaluating motion partners, highlighting comprehensive solutions and co-engineering support to simplify the path from prototype to volume production. It will be in Room 203.
  • Tactile Sensing Solutions for the Physical AI Era: This panel will include insights from Eric Utley, an applications engineering manager at Protolabs; Ron Zukerman, the director of business development and innovation at VPG; Andrew Gosline, a senior mechatronic systems engineer at Simplexity Product Development; and Dorota Shortell, the CEO of Simplexity Product Development. These experts will discuss how tactile sensing is evolving. It will take place in Room 204.

Plan your afternoon at RoboBusiness 2026

At 12:15 p.m., Bhavana Chandrashekhar, the senior manager of applied science at Amazon Robotics, and Joyce Sidopoulos, co-founder and chief of operations at MassRobotics, will start the Women in Robotics Luncheon. This ticketed event will include a fireside chat between the two tech leaders. It presents an opportunity for women in the industry to form connections, deepen relationships, and champion increased female representation in robotics leadership.

RoboBusiness 2026 beakout sessions will resume in the afternoon. Sessions starting at 1:15 p.m. include:

  • From Models to Machines: Building the Open Infrastructure for Physical AI: Nagesh Puppala, the general manager of physical AI and robotics at Intel, will explore the infrastructure required to move physical AI from prototype to production in real-world robotics systems. The talk will be in Room 209/210.
  • State of Robotics Investments: Sanjay Aggarwal, a venture partner at F-Prime Capital, and Betsy Mulé, a principal at F-Prime, will unveil the firm’s annual “State of Robotics Investments” report, highlighting the latest funding trends, emerging technology categories, and the sectors attracting the most investor interest. The session will take place in Room 207.
  • Closing the Capability Gap: A Leadership Framework for Scaling Field Robotics: Kenrick Tjandra, the robot deployment lead of Raise Robotics, will provide attendees with a decision rule for allocating engineering capacity, a vocabulary for two hidden failure modes, and the pre-mobilization gates that keep field programs from stalling. He will explain the discipline that separates a demo from a system that scales. His talk will be in Room 206.
  • Beyond the Pilot: What It Takes to Put Humanoids to Work in Manufacturing: Dr. Weiwei Chen, the founder and CEO of EmbodyX, will share what the company has learned deploying humanoids in real manufacturing environments. This RoboBusiness 2026 session will be in Room 203.
  • How Robotics and Physical AI are Transforming Modular Data Center Construction: Ali Raja, the vice president of data centers at ABB Robotics, will explore how robotics, prefabrication and modular construction can work together to streamline delivery, reduce pressure on scarce labor and scale data center capacity. The talk will be in Room 204.

Talks starting at 2:15 p.m. include:

  • Physical AI Doesn’t Have a Data Problem; It Has a Deployment Problem: Rudy Cohen, the co-founder and CEO of Inbolt, will reframe where physical AI actually pays off. Cohen said this happens not in bigger models, but in closing the loop at servo frequency and collapsing the months of fixtures, wiring, and retuning that make every deployment a six-figure project. This will take place in Room 209/210.
  • The Economics of Robotics: Is This Business Viable? Jack Pearson, an investment principal at RoboStrategy, will offer a set of mental models for judging whether a robotics business can create real value and capture it in a way that lasts. The session will be in Room 207.
  • Lessons Learned Building Reliable Outdoor Robots: This panel will feature insights from Ben Waters, co-founder and CEO of WiBotic; Vibhor Sood, co-founder and VP of engineering at Burro; Derek Chase, the vice president of robotics and AI at Nextpower; and Ben Choster, the founder of Catalyze Robotics. The panel will demonstrate how engineering decisions impact reliability, uptime, operational efficiency, and total cost of ownership. It will take place in Room 206.
  • A Crash Course in Force & Torque Sensing for Humanoids: Robert Brooks, the founder and CEO of ForceN, will summarize learnings from working with many of world’s top humanoid companies over the past three years. His talk will be in Room 203.
  • Functional Safety for Humanoid Actuators: Jordan Schaeffer, the manager of business development at Novanta, will explore how safe motion, torque control, fault detection, and actuator-level safety functions can help reduce risk while maintaining performance. The talk will take place in Room 204.

RoboBusiness 2026 talks starting at 3:30 p.m. include:

  • How Agentic Coding Empowers Lean Teams to Build Faster: Anthony Jules, the co-founder and chief innovation officer at Robust AI, will explore how AI agents are transforming the robotics development lifecycle right from the initial design phase. The talk will be in Room 209/210.
  • The RaaS Playbook: Pricing, Service & Scale: This panel will include insights from Rick Faulk, the CEO of Locus Robotics; Bill Booth, who leads technology sales, marketing, and business development at Roboworx; and Alex Linde, the chief product officer at Aescape. The speakers will provide attendees with practical strategies for building sustainable RaaS offerings that deliver value for both robotics providers and their customers. The panel will take place in Room 207.
  • Designing Dexterous Learning Robots for Outdoor Labor: Brent Shedd, the founder and CEO of AgRobotics, will deliver a practitioner-level framework: What’s working, what’s hard, and what a realistic path to commercial deployment actually looks like. The talk will be in Room 206.
  • Can Humanoids be Safe? Benjamin Twombly, the founder and CEO of Critical Systems Analysis, will share insights into both the continuity and the evolution of safety thinking as it adapts to intelligent, human-like machines operating in dynamic, real-world contexts. His session will take place in Room 203.
  • What AI-Defined Automation Looks Like in Production: François Giguére, the chief technology officer at Vention, will give attendees a framework for evaluating AI-defined automation in their own operations. The talk will be in Room 204.

Engineering Theater talks

On the show floor, we’ll be running talks in the Engineering Theater throughout the day. The talks include:

  • Sensor Solutions for Humanoids: Tools to Build the Future: Uma Krishnamoorthy, the senior director of core technology at InvenSense, will explore sensing solutions enabling today’s humanoid innovations. Her talk will start at 11:00 a.m.
  • The Robot Out of the Cage. Advanced Functional Safety for Humanoids: Jan Kaiser, the head of marketing at Synapticon, will discuss how certifiable safety architecture will lay a path towards real-world deployments for humanoids. The talk will start at 11:45 a.m.
  • From First Flash to Field Repair: Servicing Robots From a Tablet: Reed Giovannetti, co-founder and CEO of DeviceNexus, will work through the engineering questions behind keeping robots running, on the bench and in the field. This session will begin at 12:30 p.m.
  • Simulation Said Go. The Binary Said No: Keeping Robots Inside Their Requirements in the AI Era: Stojan Gancev, the VP of R&D at Aurora Labs, will discuss the importance of reasoning straight from the architecture, from the compiled binary sitting on the target processor, rather than trusting review and simulation to catch what they structurally cannot see. It will start at 2:00 p.m.
  • Shared Spaces: Navigating Challenges for Indoor Robots: This RoboBusiness 2026 panel session will include insights from Aaron Edsinger, co-founder and CEO of Hello Robot, and Matt Anderson, co-founder and CEO of A&K Robotics. The two will discuss how solving navigation challenges will be critical to achieving broad consumer acceptance and large-scale deployment. It will start at 3:30 p.m.

item.title: Gecko Robotics secures $300M contract with the U.S. Navy
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Gecko claimed this signals the Pentagon’s confidence that it is a core military capability that is delivering results.

The post Gecko Robotics secures $300M contract with the U.S. Navy appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Gecko’s suite of technologies ensures data integrity by collecting and integrating full-coverage, high-fidelity data layers. | Source: Gecko Robotics

Gecko Robotics this week said it has earned an additional $300 million its contract with the U.S. Navy and General Services Administration. With the increase, the U.S. Navy and GSA have quadrupled the ceiling value on Gecko’s contract for slashing maintenance delays and improving fleet readiness. The news came just six months after an initial $71 million IDIQ contract award.

This fourfold expansion will accommodate rapid robotic deployment across the Navy and is one of the strongest public endorsements yet of operational AI and robotics in defense, claimed Gecko Robotics. The Pittsburgh-based company claimed that this showed the Pentagon’s confidence that it is delivering a core military capability of producing results, not experimental technology.

“The conversation around AI and robotics in defense is no longer about experimental technology. It’s about delivering measurable and impactful returns,” said Jake Loosararian, co-founder and CEO of Gecko Robotics.

“With savings of millions of dollars per ship, months of inspections turning into days, and warships returning to sea faster, the U.S. Navy is demonstrating to the world how to deploy technology at scale,” he added. “We’re proud to give our service members the tools they need to stay ahead of emerging threats.”

Gecko said its AI and robotic technology can save the U.S. Navy up to $8 million in repair costs per ship and return vessels to sea quicker. It does this by identifying structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional methods, reducing inspections from months to days.

Komodo scans through deck coating without stripping them

Central to the expansion is Komodo, a proprietary Gecko robotic technology system. Komodo scans through thick, non-skid deck coatings without stripping or damaging them, giving the Navy the ability to see the health of assets without taking it apart.

It produces a full-deck heatmap of corrosion and material thickness, enabling repair teams to pinpoint damage and plan work before a ship enters drydock, which was previously possible only after maintenance had begun.

The ceiling increase comes as the Department of the Navy places greater emphasis on fleet readiness as a national security priority. Each additional day a warship spends in maintenance reduces its ability to deter adversaries, respond to crises, and project power around the world, said the Navy. The chief of naval operations has set a target of 80% fleet readiness, which Gecko will have a crucial role in helping to meet.

Gecko’s wall-climbing robots, drones, and fixed-sensors collect an unprecedented amount of data on the health of U.S. Navy ships and submarines, including components, hulls, decks and welds, with AI being used to create accurate models to identify any current and future structural issues, even ones that cannot be seen by the human eye.
